title: Workforce device management and inventory
status_rationale: Echelon's headcount, devices and device policies are not established in any record reviewed (current-state brief).
target_answer: Every device that accesses Echelon systems is enrolled in device management before it can authenticate: the workforce identity provider grants access only to compliant, enrolled devices (conditional access). Management enforces OS updates within defined windows, screen lock, firewall, full disk encryption, EDR presence and remote wipe. The device inventory is produced by the management system and reconciled to the personnel roster daily so that offboarded users' devices are wiped or returned. Access to customer data from devices is minimized by design (ANS-END-004).
current_practice: Unknown; no evidence located. Echelon is an early-stage LLC; whether any device management exists is not documented.
intended_practice: Select device management and a workforce IdP that supports device-compliance conditions; enroll all devices before customer data exists.
customer_statement: Echelon does not currently have documented workforce device management. It plans to require enrolled, compliant devices for all access before handling customer data.
open_questions: How many people and devices does Echelon have, and are any devices currently managed?
Which workforce identity provider and device management product will be used?

title: Endpoint detection and response and malware protection
status_rationale: No evidence of endpoint protection; no security operations function exists.
target_answer: All managed workforce devices run an EDR agent reporting to a monitored console, with tamper protection; alerts are triaged by a named function or managed detection provider within defined times. The bigger control is architectural: workforce devices do not hold customer data or production credentials (ANS-END-004, ANS-END-005), so a compromised laptop yields a session to a brokered, recorded, expiring access path rather than data or keys. Developer and AI agent work happens in ephemeral cloud environments rather than on the laptop.
intended_practice: Deploy EDR with device management; decide in-house versus managed detection.
customer_statement: Echelon has no documented endpoint protection program today. It plans EDR on all managed devices and to keep customer data and production credentials off workforce devices.
open_questions: Who will monitor EDR alerts, and with what response time commitment?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want compromised employee devices detected and contained before they lead to a breach of customer data.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Malware on an employee laptop steals credentials or customer data.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: EDR detects many commodity threats but misses targeted attacks and requires staffed triage; on a very small team alerts may go unread.
challenge.legally_required: Not by statute for Echelon. Some financial regulations require controls against malicious code at covered entities, which flow to vendors contractually.
challenge.contractually_required: Many questionnaires ask a yes/no EDR question, sometimes naming specific products.
challenge.historical_convention: Antivirus on every endpoint was a baseline expectation for decades.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Keeping data and production credentials off endpoints and using ephemeral cloud workspaces removes most of what endpoint compromise could reach.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Conditional access denies non-compliant devices automatically.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Device compliance state and access logs are continuous.
challenge.stronger_alternative: EDR plus architectural data minimization on endpoints.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, through device compliance reports and evidence that production access is brokered.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: High for EDR presence; architecture is additional depth, not a substitute, in customers' eyes.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If engineers download customer data or hold long-lived production credentials locally.
challenge.conventional_cost: EDR licensing per device plus triage labor.
challenge.alternative_cost: Ephemeral cloud workspaces: compute cost and setup.
challenge.alternative_risks: Browser session theft still allows abuse of brokered sessions while they are active.
supporting_arguments: Limits damage regardless of detection quality.
Fits a small team without a 24x7 SOC.
opposing_arguments: EDR remains expected and cheap; omitting it would fail many questionnaires.
Session tokens on endpoints remain valuable to attackers.

title: Device disk encryption, lock and lost device response
target_answer: Full disk encryption using the operating system's built-in encryption is enforced by device management on every managed laptop and desktop, with recovery keys escrowed to the management system and not to the user. Screen lock after a short idle period, firmware passwords or secure boot where supported, and remote lock and wipe are enforced. Lost or stolen devices are reported within one business day, wiped remotely and evaluated as a potential security incident; because devices do not hold customer data by design, loss is normally not a reportable data breach, and the encryption status record supports that determination.
intended_practice: Enforce via device management; record encryption status as evidence.
customer_statement: Echelon plans to enforce full disk encryption and remote wipe on all workforce devices; this is not yet documented as in place.
open_questions: Which state breach notification safe harbors for encrypted data would apply to a lost device, and does counsel accept device encryption status records as evidence?

title: Personal devices, contractor devices and data on endpoints
status_rationale: No BYOD or contractor device policy located; Echelon's use of contractors and agents is described in the business plan as intended, not operated.
target_answer: Personal and contractor-owned devices may access only low-sensitivity collaboration tools through a managed browser profile or application protection policy that blocks download, copy and local storage of Echelon data. Access to customer data and production (including support diagnostics) is allowed only from Echelon-managed devices through the brokered access path. Customer data is never downloaded to endpoints; exports are delivered to the customer through the platform rather than via employees. Contractors are bound by the same device conditions in their agreements.
intended_practice: Write the policy and enforce it through IdP conditional access before contractors are engaged on customer-data work.
customer_statement: Echelon plans to prohibit access to customer data from personal or unmanaged devices. No policy is in place today.
open_questions: Will Echelon use contractors for engineering or support, and will they use their own devices?

title: Developer workstation and AI coding agent sandbox security
status_rationale: Echelon engineering relies heavily on AI agents; Praxis records agent provenance for repository work (praxis@12bf9951), but no workstation or agent sandbox policy exists, and no production exists for agents to reach.
target_answer: Software is developed in ephemeral, cloud-hosted workspaces rather than on laptops where possible. AI coding agents run in isolated sandboxes with: no production credentials or production data; network egress limited to source control, package registries through a controlled proxy, and approved model endpoints; repository-scoped, short-lived source control tokens; no ability to push to protected branches, approve their own changes, or modify CI and release configuration without human approval; and every agent execution recorded with agent identity, model, task and resulting commits (Praxis provenance). Agent-written changes pass the same review and release gates as human changes, and control-relevant modules require two human approvers (CNV-PLT-010). Secrets never enter agent context; secret scanning runs on every commit (ECTL-ENC-008). Package installs in sandboxes resolve only through the approved dependency policy (SEC-SUPPLY-001).
current_practice: Praxis provides agent provenance records in repository front matter and execution records (observed in this repository's AGENTS.md). Agents operate in vendor-hosted environments whose configuration is not governed by an Echelon policy. No Echelon sandbox standard exists.
intended_practice: Write an agent sandbox standard; restrict agent tokens; make protected-branch and CI-config changes require human approval.
provable: Praxis provenance records exist for repository work (first-party, not independently verified). Nothing proves sandbox isolation, egress limits or credential scoping.
customer_statement: Echelon's Praxis tooling exists and records agent provenance for repository work, but it is not operated for a production service. A formal sandbox standard limiting agent credentials, network access and authority is planned and not yet established.
residual_risks: Prompt injection through repository content, issues or dependencies can steer an agent within its granted authority.
Agent vendors' own infrastructure is a fourth party whose controls Echelon relies on.
open_questions: Which agent platforms will be approved for Echelon engineering, and do their sandboxes allow Echelon to set egress and credential policy?
Should agent sandbox providers be treated as subservice organizations once production code is built with them?
